name: Ymir
shortDescription: The first being. From his corpse the world was made.
sources: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Gylfaginning (Iceland, c. 1220)
Poetic Edda: Vafþrúðnismál, stanzas 21 and 28-35
Poetic Edda: Grímnismál, stanzas 40-41

chainSummary.claim: Ymir's name means "Scream": the primordial scream in the void, so that the giant out of whose body the Norse world was built is named for the sound of the beginning.
chainSummary.verdict: The Old Norse texts that name Ymir give the name and one alternative name for him and do not say what either means; the reading "Scream" is a modern argument about what a medieval audience would have heard in the word, published in 2003 and picked up from there.

name: Nephilim
shortDescription: The mighty ones of old: offspring of the sons of God and daughters of men.
sources: Genesis 6:1-4; Numbers 13:33 (Hebrew Bible)
1 Enoch, the Book of the Watchers, chapters 6-16 (3rd-1st c. BCE)
Book of Jubilees 5; Dead Sea Scrolls Enoch fragments
Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews I.3.1 (tradition); V.2.3 / 5.125 (bones at Hebron)
imageAlt: The Nephilim, mighty ones of old

chainSummary.claim: The nephilim of Genesis 6 were giants: enormous hybrid offspring born when the sons of God took human wives, whose kind the Israelite spies later saw and felt like grasshoppers beside.
chainSummary.verdict: The giant reading is genuinely ancient and continuously attested, but it travels on translation and on expansion literature rather than on the wording of the Hebrew verse.

name: Goliath of Gath
height: Six cubits and a span (Masoretic); four cubits and a span (Dead Sea Scrolls)
shortDescription: The Philistine champion of Gath who fell to a shepherd's stone.
sources: 1 Samuel 17 (Masoretic Text); Septuagint 1 Kingdoms 17 (shorter version)
2 Samuel 21:19 and 1 Chronicles 20:5 (the Elhanan problem)
4QSam-a, Dead Sea Scrolls (height variant)
Tell es-Safi/Gath ostracon, 10th-9th c. BCE (Philistine names)

chainSummary.claim: Goliath of Gath stood six cubits and a span, about nine feet nine inches, or close to three metres.
chainSummary.verdict: The height is a textual variant rather than a fixed number: the surviving copies of 1 Samuel 17:4 do not agree with each other, and the disagreement is ancient.

name: Og of Bashan
height: Implied by iron bed: ~9 cubits long
shortDescription: Last of the Rephaim; king of Bashan whose iron bed was a wonder.
sources: Deuteronomy 3:1-13 (the iron bedstead at Rabbah); Numbers 21:33-35
Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 54b, Niddah 24b, and Niddah 61a (rabbinic expansion)
Ugaritic rpum texts (comparative evidence for the term)
imageAlt: Og of Bashan, last of the Rephaim

chainSummary.claim: Deuteronomy records that Og of Bashan's iron bed was nine cubits long and four wide, and that measurement proves Og himself stood about four metres, roughly thirteen and a half feet.
chainSummary.verdict: The four metre figure is the length of an object, not a stated height: the verse measures the bed and leaves the man unmeasured, and the readers who converted bed into body disagreed with each other about how to do it.

name: Atlas
shortDescription: Titan condemned to hold the sky upon his shoulders.
sources: Hesiod, Theogony 517-520 and 746-748 (c. 700 BCE)
Homer, Odyssey I.52-54
Apollodorus, Bibliotheca II.5.11 (the golden apples)
Ovid, Metamorphoses IV.627-662 (petrification by Perseus)

name: Polyphemus
shortDescription: The one-eyed Cyclops who trapped Odysseus in his cave.
sources: Homer, Odyssey IX.105-566
Euripides, Cyclops (satyr play, 5th c. BCE)
Theocritus, Idylls VI and XI
Ovid, Metamorphoses XIII.750-897 (Polyphemus, Galatea and Acis)

chainSummary.claim: The trick in Odyssey 9, where Odysseus gives his name as Nobody and then blinds the Cyclops and escapes under the sheep, was invented by Homer for the poem, and the folk versions collected later across Europe and Asia are descendants of it.
chainSummary.verdict: The surviving documents split the claim rather than settling it: the blinding and the escape under the flock are attested in traditions that scholars have long declined to derive from the poem, while the false name is argued about on separate grounds, and recent work warns against reconstructing what stood behind Homer at all.

name: Enceladus
shortDescription: Giant buried beneath Sicily; his thrashing is said to cause earthquakes.
sources: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca I.6.1-2 (the Gigantomachy)
Virgil, Aeneid III.578-582 (Enceladus beneath Etna)
Hesiod, Theogony 185 (birth of the Giants from Gaia)
Pergamon Altar frieze, 2nd c. BCE (Berlin): major visual source

name: Antaeus
shortDescription: Libyan giant who drew strength from the earth: until Heracles lifted him.
sources: Pindar, Isthmian IV
Apollodorus, Bibliotheca II.5.11
Lucan, Pharsalia IV.590-660
Plutarch, Life of Sertorius 9 (the alleged skeleton at Tingis)

name: Alcyoneus
shortDescription: Immortal on his native soil; slain only when dragged beyond its border.
sources: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca I.6.1
Pindar, Nemean IV and Isthmian VI
Pergamon Altar frieze, east side, 2nd c. BCE (Berlin)

name: Porphyrion
shortDescription: King of the Gigantes who assailed Hera and fell to Zeus and Heracles.
sources: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca I.6.2
Pindar, Pythian VIII.12-18
Pergamon Altar frieze, 2nd c. BCE (Berlin)

name: Polybotes
shortDescription: Pursued by Poseidon across the sea; crushed under the island of Nisyros.
sources: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca I.6.2
Strabo, Geography X.5.16 (Nisyros and its volcanic character)
Attic vase painting of the Gigantomachy, 6th-5th c. BCE

name: Briareus
shortDescription: Hundred-handed giant who aided Zeus against the Titans.
sources: Hesiod, Theogony 147-153, 617-735
Homer, Iliad I.396-406 (Briareus called up to Olympus)
Pausanias, Description of Greece II.1.6 and II.4.7 (Corinthian tradition)
Apollodorus, Bibliotheca I.1-2

name: Orion
shortDescription: The hunter so great he was set among the stars.
sources: Homer, Odyssey XI.572-575; Iliad XVIII.486-489
Hesiod, Works and Days 598-616 (Orion as agricultural calendar)
Apollodorus, Bibliotheca I.4.3-5 (competing accounts of his death)
Hyginus, Astronomica II.34; Pseudo-Eratosthenes, Catasterismi 32

name: Geryon
shortDescription: Three-bodied giant of the far west whose cattle Heracles stole.
sources: Hesiod, Theogony 287-294, 979-983
Stesichorus, Geryoneis (6th c. BCE, surviving in fragments)
Apollodorus, Bibliotheca II.5.10
Attic vase painting, 6th c. BCE; Dante, Inferno XVII (medieval reinvention)

name: Tityus
shortDescription: Giant punished in the underworld; vultures feast forever on his liver.
sources: Homer, Odyssey XI.576-581
Apollodorus, Bibliotheca I.4.1
Pindar, Pythian IV.90-92
Lucretius, De Rerum Natura III.984-994 (rationalising reading)

name: Talos
shortDescription: The bronze guardian of Crete: automaton giant with a single vein of ichor.
sources: Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica IV.1638-1688
Apollodorus, Bibliotheca I.9.26
Attic red-figure krater, 4th c. BCE (the death of Talos)
Minos 320c (transmitted under Plato's name; authorship disputed): the rationalised, law-carrying Talos

name: Thrym
shortDescription: Frost giant who stole Mjölnir and demanded Freyja as bride.
sources: Poetic Edda: Þrymskviða (Codex Regius, 13th c.)
Later Scandinavian ballad tradition (Danish, Swedish, Norwegian variants)

name: Hrungnir
shortDescription: Stone-hearted giant who dueled Thor and left a whetstone in his head.
sources: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Skáldskaparmál 17
Þjóðólfr of Hvinir, Haustlöng (9th-10th c., quoted by Snorri)

name: Skrymir
shortDescription: The vast wanderer whose glove was a hall: master of illusions.
sources: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Gylfaginning 44-47
Saxo Grammaticus, Gesta Danorum VIII (the Utgarthilocus episode)

name: Bestla
shortDescription: Frost-giantess mother of Odin: the gods' giant bloodline.
sources: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Gylfaginning 6
Poetic Edda: Hávamál 140 (the son of Bölthorn)

name: Balor
shortDescription: Fomorian king whose eye destroyed armies: slain by his grandson Lugh.
sources: Cath Maige Tuired (The Second Battle of Mag Tuired), Old/Middle Irish
Lebor Gabala Erenn (Book of Invasions)
Donegal and Tory Island oral tradition, collected 19th-20th c.

chainSummary.claim: Balor and the second battle of Mag Tuired come down to us from pre-Christian Irish tradition: the story is native Irish pagan myth, carried orally through the conversion and only later written down by monks.
chainSummary.verdict: The witnesses checked for this ladder are Christian-era Irish manuscripts and post-medieval collections, and the case for older material inside them rests on linguistic dating and comparison rather than on a document from pagan Ireland.

name: Cormoran
shortDescription: Cornish giant of St Michael's Mount, felled by Jack the Giant Killer.
sources: Jack the Giant Killer chapbooks (earliest known ed. c. 1711)
Robert Hunt, Popular Romances of the West of England (1865)
William Bottrell, Traditions and Hearthside Stories of West Cornwall (1870-80)
Joseph Jacobs, English Fairy Tales (1890)

name: Gogmagog
shortDescription: British giant who wrestled Corineus and gave his name to London's guardians.
sources: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae I.16 (c. 1136)
Wace, Roman de Brut (1155); Layamon, Brut (c. 1200)
London Guildhall civic records and Lord Mayor's pageant tradition, 15th c. onward
Ezekiel 38-39; Revelation 20:8 (the biblical names)

chainSummary.claim: Gogmagog was the last giant of Albion, thrown from the cliffs at Plymouth by Corineus after losing a wrestling match.
chainSummary.verdict: The wrestling match and the fall from a cliff are attested in a twelfth-century Latin history, but that text puts the fight at the shore where Brutus landed rather than at Plymouth, and the Plymouth address is supplied by later documents.

name: Jentilak
shortDescription: Basque giants of the mountains who built megaliths and fled the new faith.
sources: José Miguel de Barandiarán, Basque mythology fieldwork and collections (20th c.)
Resurrección María de Azkue, Euskalerriaren Yakintza (1935-47)
Basque and Navarrese megalithic place-names (jentiletxe, jentilarri)
Anton Erkoreka, Los gentiles: el mito de los gigantes en el País Vasco, Cuadernos de Etnología y Etnografía de Navarra 23 (1976)
Anuntxi Arana, Euskal mitologiaz: jentilak eta kristauak (2008)
Emilio Xabier Dueñas, 'El carbonero Olentzero y el obispo (San) Nicolás', Eusko Ikaskuntza, Lankidetzan 41

name: Olentzero
shortDescription: The Basque charcoal-burner of Christmas: last echo of the jentilak.
sources: Basque oral tradition via Barandiarán and Azkue collections
Olentzero song texts, 19th c. onward, with regional variants
20th-c. Basque cultural documentation of the modern gift-bringer role
imageAlt: Olentzero on a snowbound hillside at night, a sack over one shoulder and a staff in hand, bare oaks behind him and a charcoal fire burning on the far slope

name: Ravana
shortDescription: Ten-headed king of Lanka: scholar, devotee, abductor of Sita.
sources: Valmiki, Ramayana (Sanskrit); Uttara Kanda for the boon and Kailasa episode
Tulsidas, Ramcharitmanas (Awadhi, 16th c.)
Ramakien (Thai) and Reamker (Cambodian) regional recensions
Shiva Tandava Stotram, traditionally attributed to Ravana

chainSummary.claim: Every year at Dussehra, right across India, towering effigies of Ravana are packed with fireworks and set alight to mark the victory of good over evil.
chainSummary.verdict: The burning is thoroughly documented as a present-day practice, but the written trail for it thins fast as you go back, and the 'across India' half of the claim is contradicted by places that document their refusal to do it.

name: Kumbhakarna
shortDescription: Ravana's giant brother who slept six months and woke to war.
sources: Valmiki, Ramayana: Yuddha Kanda (the waking and the battle)
Valmiki, Ramayana: Uttara Kanda (the boon)
Tulsidas, Ramcharitmanas (Awadhi, 16th c.)
Ramlila performance tradition, North India

name: Hiranyakashipu
shortDescription: Asura king who could not be killed by man or beast: until Narasimha.
sources: Bhagavata Purana, Canto 7 (Prahlada and Narasimha)
Vishnu Purana, Book 1; Narasimha Purana
South Indian temple sculpture, Narasimha cycle

name: Mahabali
shortDescription: Generous asura king sent to the underworld by Vamana's three steps.
sources: Bhagavata Purana, Canto 8 (the Vamana avatar)
Rigveda 1.154 (Vishnu's three strides, without Bali)
Vamana Purana
Malayalam Onam folk verses ('Maveli nadu vaneedum kalam')

name: Svyatogor
shortDescription: Mountain-strong bogatyr who could not be lifted by the earth itself.
sources: Russian byliny, Onega and Karelian oral tradition
Pavel Rybnikov, Songs Collected by P.N. Rybnikov (1861-67)
Alexander Gilferding, Onega Byliny (1873)

name: Quinametzin
shortDescription: Giant race of a previous sun who built great structures and fell to divine order.
sources: Fernando de Alva Ixtlilxochitl, Relaciones and Historia de la nacion chichimeca (late 16th-early 17th c.)
Bernardino de Sahagun, Florentine Codex (16th c.)
Diego Duran, Historia de las Indias de Nueva Espana
Pleistocene megafauna deposits, Valley of Mexico (physical context)
imageAlt: Quinametzin, giants of a previous sun

name: Xelhua
shortDescription: Giant survivor of the flood who raised the great pyramid of Cholula.
sources: Diego Duran, Historia de las Indias de Nueva Espana (16th c.)
Alexander von Humboldt, Vues des Cordilleres (1810): transmission and amplification
Archaeological survey of the Great Pyramid of Cholula, 1930s onward

name: Kua Fu
shortDescription: The giant who chased the sun and died of thirst: staff becoming a forest.
sources: Shanhaijing (Classic of Mountains and Seas), Dahuang Beijing and Haiwai Beijing sections
Liezi, Tangwen chapter
Guo Pu, commentary on the Shanhaijing (4th c. CE)

name: Fangfeng
height: Giant (one of the tallest in lore)
shortDescription: Giant executed by Yu the Great for arriving late to the flood assembly.
sources: Guoyu (Discourses of the States), Lu yu section (Confucius and the bones)
Sima Qian, Shiji, Annals of Xia (c. 91 BCE)
Local gazetteers of the Kuaiji/Deqing region, Zhejiang

name: Oni
shortDescription: Horned ogres of Japanese folklore: punishers, marauders, festival demons.
sources: Konjaku Monogatarishu (late Heian period tale collection)
Otogizoshi illustrated tales (Muromachi period)
Kamakura-period Buddhist hell scrolls (iconographic source)
Setsubun observance, documented from the Muromachi period

name: Shuten Dōji
shortDescription: Demon king of Mount Ōe: drunkard oni slain by Raikō's band.
sources: Oeyama ekotoba (illustrated handscroll, Nanbokuchō / Muromachi period (14th c.))
Otogizoshi versions of the Shuten-doji tale
Noh and kabuki adaptations; ukiyo-e treatments incl. Tsukioka Yoshitoshi
imageAlt: Shuten Dōji, demon king of Mount Ōe

chainSummary.claim: Shuten-doji is an ancient Japanese demon of the Heian period: the oni chief of Mount Oe who preyed on Kyoto until Minamoto no Yorimitsu killed him around the turn of the eleventh century.
chainSummary.verdict: The Heian dating belongs to the story's setting rather than to the documents that carry it, and the distance between the two is where this claim lives.

name: Dzunukwa
shortDescription: Giantess of the woods who steals children and owns treasures of copper and power.
sources: Kwakwaka'wakw oral tradition and hereditary mask traditions
Franz Boas with George Hunt, Kwakiutl ethnographic corpus (late 19th-early 20th c.)
Contemporary Kwakwaka'wakw carvers and community sources
imageAlt: Dzunukwa, Wild Woman of the Woods

name: Si-Te-Cah
shortDescription: A Northern Paiute tradition about a people-eating tribe, and how it became a story about giants.
sources: Sarah Winnemucca Hopkins, Life Among the Piutes (1883)
L.L. Loud and M.R. Harrington, Lovelock Cave, UC Publications in American Archaeology and Ethnology (1929)
Subsequent Great Basin archaeological literature
Adrienne Mayor, Fossil Legends of the First Americans (2005)
imageAlt: A tall figure at the mouth of Lovelock Cave, firelight behind him

chainSummary.claim: Excavations at Lovelock Cave in Nevada recovered the skeletons and mummies of a race of red-haired giants, the Si-Te-Cah of Paiute tradition, some of them eight to ten feet tall.
chainSummary.verdict: Red hair is attested in the record from the beginning, in Paiute tradition and in one eyewitness statement about a mummy; the giant heights enter later, through measurements taken outside the cave and through remains that were dispersed before anyone studied them.

name: Tsul 'Kalu
shortDescription: Cherokee lord of the hunt: slant-eyed giant of the mountains.
sources: James Mooney, Myths of the Cherokee, BAE 19th Annual Report (1900)
Cherokee oral tradition (Eastern Band; Cherokee Nation)
Judaculla Rock petroglyph site, Jackson County, North Carolina

chainSummary.claim: Tsul'kalu, the slant-eyed giant who owns the game animals, is a genuine figure of old Cherokee tradition, remembered in the mountains of western North Carolina and marked on the stone now called Judaculla Rock.
chainSummary.verdict: The tradition is documented in nineteenth-century print and rests mainly on a turn-of-the-century ethnographic report whose Cherokee narrators are named, while the carved rock associated with him is much older than that writing and is linked to him by tradition rather than by anything in the stone.

name: Kee-Wakw
shortDescription: Ice-hearted cannibal giant of northern forests: a winter horror.
sources: Abenaki and wider Wabanaki oral tradition (variation by community)
Charles G. Leland, Algonquin Legends of New England (1884): use with caution
Frank Speck, Penobscot and related ethnographic work, early 20th c.
Contemporary Wabanaki authors, incl. Joseph Bruchac

name: Gaoh
shortDescription: Master of the winds: a giant spirit who pens the gales.
sources: Haudenosaunee oral tradition, Six Nations (variation between nations)
Harriet Maxwell Converse, Myths and Legends of the New York State Iroquois (1908), ed. A.C. Parker
Arthur C. Parker, Seneca ethnographic and folkloric writings, early 20th c.

name: Budj Bim Giants
alsoKnownAs: Associated with Budj Bim / Tyrendarra country
shortDescription: Ancestral beings of giant scale in the volcanic landscape of Budj Bim.
sources: Gunditjmara tradition, via Gunditj Mirring Traditional Owners Aboriginal Corporation
UNESCO World Heritage inscription, Budj Bim Cultural Landscape (2019)
Published argon-argon dating of the Budj Bim eruption
Archaeological literature on the Budj Bim aquaculture systems
AIATSIS protocols for Indigenous knowledge

shortDescription: One-eyed giant spirits of Tiwi tradition who hunt with clubs and bags.

Contemporary Tiwi art centres: Tiwi Design, Jilamara, Munupi

shortDescription: Giant figure in northern Australian story cycles of pursuit and country.

AIATSIS protocols for Indigenous knowledge

shortDescription: Cannibal giant of southeastern Aboriginal tales: a terror of the camp edge.
sources: Australian Aboriginal oral tradition (community not reliably identified)
20th-c. legend compilations: unreliable, see disputed
AIATSIS protocols for Indigenous knowledge

shortDescription: Giant being in Aboriginal narrative: sparse in print, strong in place.

name: Maero
shortDescription: Wild folk of the forest in Māori tradition: long fingers, fierce, untamed.
sources: Maori oral tradition (varies by iwi)
John White, The Ancient History of the Maori (1887-90): period-bound
Elsdon Best, ethnographic writings on Maori forest lore, early 20th c.
Te Ara: The Encyclopedia of New Zealand

name: Kahui-Tipua
shortDescription: Bands of supernatural giants in Māori tradition: tipua of collective power.
sources: Southern Māori oral tradition (Ngāi Tahu; earlier Waitaha and Kati Mamoe)
Herries Beattie, "Nature-lore of the Southern Maori", Transactions and Proceedings of the New Zealand Institute 52 (1920)
Ngāi Tahu published sources and Claims Settlement documentation
Te Ara: The Encyclopedia of New Zealand
James W. Stack, "Sketch of the Traditional History of the South Island Maoris", Transactions and Proceedings of the New Zealand Institute 10 (1877)

name: Nawao
shortDescription: Wild people of early Aotearoa tradition: forest dwellers of great strength.
sources: Māori oral tradition (varies by iwi; not a single canonical account)
19th-c. settler-era compilations - preserved and distorted the material; treat with caution
Later scholarship rejecting the pre-Māori settlement thesis

name: Amazimu
shortDescription: Cannibal ogres of Zulu and related folklore: shape-shifting eaters of the unwary.
sources: Zulu and Nguni oral tradition (izinganekwane, intsomi genres)
Henry Callaway, Nursery Tales, Traditions, and Histories of the Zulus (1868)
Harold Scheub, studies of Xhosa and Zulu oral performance (1960s onward)

name: Giant of the Forest
shortDescription: West African forest giant of tale cycles: a being of the deep bush.
sources: Hausa oral tradition (tatsuniyoyi), northern Nigeria and Niger
Frank Edgar, Litafi na Tatsuniyoyi na Hausa (1911-13)
Neil Skinner, Hausa Tales and Traditions (partial translation of Edgar)

name: Stallo
shortDescription: Sámi giant-troll of the north: strong, dull-witted, dangerous to herders.
sources: Sámi oral tradition, N. Norway, Sweden, Finland and Kola
Johan Turi, Muitalus sámiid birra (1910)
J.K. Qvigstad, Lappiske eventyr og sagn (1927-29)
Eldar Heide, 'The Wild Host and the Etymology of Sami Stállu and Norwegian Ståle(sferda): Reflecting Ancient Contact', Arv 75 (2019), 73-93
J.A. Friis, Lappisk Mythologi (1871); Rolf Kjellström, Fataburen (1976)
Anders Wepsäläinen on the stállotomter (2011); Olof Holm, Fornvännen 111 (2016)
Liedgren and Bergman (2009); Bergman et al. (2008); Storli (1993-94)
Johannes Schefferus, Lapponia (1673): external account of Sámi religion, cited for collection history

chainSummary.claim: The Stállu of Sámi tradition preserves a memory of real outsiders who raided the Sámi: Norse or Christian vikings, robbers and tax collectors, whose iron-clad, plundering violence the tales record and whose abandoned mountain houses are still called Stallo sites.
chainSummary.verdict: The raider reading is an interpretation laid over the folk material by scholars, traceable in print from the 1870s, and it is still repeated in reference works while being argued against in specialist literature.

name: Ojáncanu
shortDescription: One-eyed Cantabrian giant of the forest: enemy of the good anjana.
sources: Manuel Llano, Cantabrian folk tales and regional writings (early 20th c.)
Regional folklore collections of Cantabria, 19th-20th c.
Comparative note: Homer, Odyssey IX (Polyphemus), for the one-eye motif

name: Rübezahl
shortDescription: Mountain spirit of the Riesengebirge: trickster, giant, weather-lord.
sources: Martin Helwig, map of Silesia (1561): early depiction
Johannes Praetorius, Rübezahl collections (17th c.)
J.K.A. Musäus, Volksmährchen der Deutschen, vol. 2 (1783)
Czech Krakonoš tradition, incl. Krkonošské pohádky

chainSummary.claim: Rübezahl is an ancient Germanic mountain god, a pre-Christian deity of the Giant Mountains who survived Christianisation as a folk spirit.
chainSummary.verdict: The documents on this ladder run back to the sixteenth century, where Rübezahl appears as a named mountain demon rather than as a god, and in the places where an ancient-deity reading is stated it is stated as conjecture.

name: Giant of Kandahar
shortDescription: Unverified modern military legend of a red-haired giant near Kandahar.
sources: Paranormal radio, forum, YouTube and podcast circulation (datable cluster from 2016)
Snopes inquiry to the US Department of Defense, 2016 (denial; not a FOIA docket)
Absence of corroborating US military records
Comparative: 19th-c. American giant lore and Nephilim literature

chainSummary.claim: In 2002 a US special forces patrol in the mountains of Kandahar province, Afghanistan, was attacked by a giant twelve to thirteen feet tall, red-haired, with six fingers on each hand and two rows of teeth. It killed one American with a spear before the team shot it. The body was recovered, flown out of the country, and the incident was classified.
chainSummary.verdict: The story is carried by datable broadcasts, articles and podcasts rather than by any record of an event, and the tellings on this ladder contradict one another about where the body went, when the sighting happened and who was present, while the published casualty accounting and the replies given to journalists hold nothing matching the account.

name: Giant of Kunar
shortDescription: Unverified legend of a giant observed in Kunar Province.
sources: Paranormal radio and internet forum circulation, mid-2000s onward
Cable television treatments, 2010s (amplification, not evidence)
Absence of corroborating military records

chainSummary.claim: US forces operating in the Kunar valley in Afghanistan killed a giant, took casualties doing it, recovered the body, and the evidence was classified and suppressed.
chainSummary.verdict: The documents that place a giant in Kunar describe something watched at a distance through a thermal sight, with no body and no classification, while the killing and the suppressed evidence attach to the Kandahar telling of the story.

name: Paul Bunyan
height: As tall as the tale requires
shortDescription: Lumberjack giant of American tall tales: Babe the Blue Ox at his side.
sources: Great Lakes logging-camp oral tradition, late 19th c.
James MacGillivray, Detroit News-Tribune (1910)
William Laughead, Red River Lumber Company pamphlets (1916 onward)
Richard Dorson, on fakelore (mid-20th c. critique)

name: Surtr

chainSummary.claim: Gargantua is Rabelais's invention: the giant was made up by a sixteenth-century novelist, and everything else, including the standing stones that carry his name, is downstream of the book.
chainSummary.verdict: The paper trail is thinner and more contested than either side of this argument usually admits, and the nineteenth-century scholars who built the case against Rabelais conceded its weakest point in their own pages.

chainSummary.claim: The Patagonians were a race of giants twelve to fifteen feet tall, first met by Magellan's crew at Port San Julian in 1520 and reported by European voyagers for the next two and a half centuries.
chainSummary.verdict: The voyage narratives that carry this story describe unusually tall people, but where they give numbers at all the numbers are much smaller than twelve to fifteen feet, and the figures shrink further once anyone measures.

chainSummary.claim: The giants who landed by sea at the Punta de Santa Elena were destroyed by fire that came down from heaven, a punishment the local people remembered and the Spanish chronicler Pedro Cieza de Leon wrote down in 1553.
chainSummary.verdict: The wording that carries this claim is documented in a printed chronicle of 1553, where the destruction sentence is introduced as something people say and the fire is attached to a charge of sodomy; the scholarship consulted here reads the fire and the angel as the chronicler's own framing, and the bones on the peninsula were being called animal rather than human by the end of the eighteenth century.
